precepts.text: Jacob said give me my wife that I may go in unto her, Laban made a feast and brought Leah to him, and he went in unto her; the feast is the coming together.
precepts.point: Why would a just man hide a pregnant woman he had not impregnated, and if she had committed adultery why would a just man hide her sin? There is no way around that question; he hid her because the child was his.

note.label: The Nativity: the Bloodline, Birthright, & the Messiah

precepts.why:
Matthew says Mary was espoused to Joseph, and “before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost.” What does “came together” mean? Genesis 29 shows the custom. Jacob served seven years for Rachel, then said, “Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in unto her.” “And Laban gathered together all the men of the place, and made a feast. And it came to pass in the evening, that he took Leah his daughter, and brought her to him; and he went in unto her.”

The feast is the coming together. Coming together was the customary wedding feast, the same custom seen with Tobit. So before Joseph and Mary came together in the wedding feast, they lay together. There was no fornication, because they were already espoused. Espousal is marriage: once the father made the promise, she could not go and marry another, and a man who lies with a betrothed woman commits adultery. That is why the angel called Mary Joseph's wife. She was his wife by espousal, not because he had lain with her; sex alone does not make a marriage.

Then “Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily.” The commentators say that means he meant to divorce her secretly, because the child was not his. But if a just man's espoused wife were pregnant by another man, the law said she must die; a just man would not hide her. Put her away privily means hide her, the way “Elisabeth conceived, and hid herself five months.” A public example means being put to death in public. Had Mary gone back to her father's house showing, they would have said she played the harlot, just as they said of Tamar at three months.

So here is the question: why would a just man hide a pregnant woman he did not impregnate? And if she had committed adultery, why would a just man hide her sin? There is no way around that question. Minded means he was thinking about it: he was going to hide her so nothing would happen to her for what the two of them had done, because the child was his.

precepts.text: Isaac charged Jacob to arise and go to Padanaram to the house of Bethuel; that is where Jacob was headed.
precepts.point: This is the same ground the family had already covered. Isaac charged Jacob to go to Padanaram to the house of Bethuel, and generations earlier Terah had brought Abram from Ur of the Chaldees up along the Euphrates, and they came unto Haran and dwelt there.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
Jacob “came into the land of the people of the east” because that is where he was sent. Isaac charged him: “Arise, go to Padan–aram, to the house of Bethuel thy mother’s father; and take thee a wife from thence of the daughters of Laban thy mother’s brother.”

On the map he goes north out of Canaan and then east to Haran in Padanaram. That is why the men at the well answer him, “Of Haran are we.” He had arrived where his father told him to go.

precepts.text: Terah took Abram from Ur of the Chaldees to go into Canaan, and they came unto Haran and dwelt there; Jacob's road runs back to the family's old dwelling.
precepts.point: This is the same ground the family had already covered. Isaac charged Jacob to go to Padanaram to the house of Bethuel, and generations earlier Terah had brought Abram from Ur of the Chaldees up along the Euphrates, and they came unto Haran and dwelt there.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
This is the same ground the family had already covered. Generations earlier “Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter in law, his son Abram’s wife; and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan; and they came unto Haran, and dwelt there.”

Terah brought Abram up from Ur along the Euphrates and stopped at Haran. Now Jacob, coming out of Canaan, goes north and east and finds shepherds who say, “Of Haran are we.” Jacob’s road runs back to the family’s old dwelling.

precepts.text: Terah begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran; Laban is of Nahor's line, so Jacob has come to his own people.
precepts.point: This ties the family line together: Abraham first journeyed from Ur of the Chaldees northwest to Haran, and now Jacob comes up from Canaan northeast to Haran. Because of the way Jacob traveled, he went back home and is dwelling amongst family.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
“Know ye Laban the son of Nahor?” And the men of Haran know him. “Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran.” Laban is of Nahor’s line, and he dwells in that area because the family remained there when Terah stopped at Haran.

It ties the family line together. Abraham first journeyed from Ur of the Chaldees northwest to Haran, and now Jacob comes up from Canaan northeast to Haran. Because of the way Jacob traveled, he went back home and is dwelling amongst family, the house of Nahor.

precepts.text: Abimelech told his mother's brethren, Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh; the phrase declares, we are family.
precepts.point: Laban said unto Jacob, Surely thou art my bone and my flesh. In the scriptures that phrase means we are family; Jacob abode with him a month, and Laban, because Jacob was his brother, asked what his wages should be.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem “unto his mother’s brethren” and pleaded with “all the family of the house of his mother’s father” to have him reign over them instead of the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal. His closing argument was kinship: “remember also that I am your bone and your flesh.”

That is the same phrase Laban used to Jacob: “Surely thou art my bone and my flesh.” In the scriptures it declares, we are family. Laban is owning Jacob as kin, and it is because Jacob was his brother that he would not have him serve for nought, but asked what his wages should be.

precepts.text: Ye are my brethren, ye are my bones and my flesh; further proof that bone and flesh speaks of kindred.
precepts.point: Laban said unto Jacob, Surely thou art my bone and my flesh. In the scriptures that phrase means we are family; Jacob abode with him a month, and Laban, because Jacob was his brother, asked what his wages should be.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
David reminded the elders of Judah who they were to him: “Ye are my brethren, ye are my bones and my flesh: wherefore then are ye the last to bring back the king?” He calls them brethren and bones and flesh in the same breath; the two mean the same thing.

Further proof that bone and flesh speaks of kindred. When Laban said to Jacob, “Surely thou art my bone and my flesh”, and then called him “my brother”, he was saying the same thing David said to Judah: you are my family.

precepts.text: A man loveth nothing better than the beauty of a woman; that is what Jacob saw in Rachel.
precepts.point: Do not be hasty to credit somebody based on their looks. Of course you want somebody you are attracted to, but commending a person for beauty alone gets a lot of people in trouble.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
“The beauty of a woman cheereth the countenance, and a man loveth nothing better.” That is what Jacob saw in Rachel. Leah “was tender eyed; but Rachel was beautiful and well favoured. And Jacob loved Rachel”, and his eyes had been fixed on her from the start: he ran to roll the stone from the well's mouth, watered her flock and kissed her when she came out with the sheep, and now he offers to serve seven years for her.

There is nothing strange in that. A man loveth nothing better than the beauty of a woman, and of course you want somebody you are attracted to. The scripture simply names what moved Jacob.

precepts.text: Do not be hasty to credit somebody for their beauty or their outward appearance.
precepts.point: Do not be hasty to credit somebody based on their looks. Of course you want somebody you are attracted to, but commending a person for beauty alone gets a lot of people in trouble.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
“Commend not a man for his beauty; neither abhor a man for his outward appearance.” Do not be hasty to credit somebody based on their looks.

Jacob loved Rachel because she “was beautiful and well favoured”, while Leah “was tender eyed”. Of course you want somebody you are attracted to, but commending a person for beauty alone gets a lot of people in trouble. That is the caution to carry alongside Jacob's seven years: beauty is what he saw, and it is not enough by itself to commend anyone.

precepts.text: Men let gold and silver go and fix their eyes fast on a comely woman; by this ye must know that women have dominion over you.
precepts.point: Men gather gold and silver and every goodly thing, then let all those things go and fix their eyes fast on a woman comely in favour and beauty. Many run out of their wits for a woman and become servants for their sakes; Jacob became a servant fourteen years, because he was deceived and served another seven.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
Jacob served seven years for Rachel, “and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.” That is how fine she was to him: with six and a half years still left, it felt like a couple of days. Here is why.

“Yea, and if men have gathered together gold and silver, or any other goodly thing, do they not love a woman which is comely in favour and beauty?” Men gather every goodly thing, then, “letting all those things go, do they not gape, and even with open mouth fix their eyes fast on her”. And “have not all men more desire unto her than unto silver or gold, or any goodly thing whatsoever?” “A man leaveth his own father that brought him up, and his own country, and cleaveth unto his wife”, and “remembereth neither father, nor mother, nor country.”

The conclusion is plain: “By this also ye must know that women have dominion over you: do ye not labour and toil, and give and bring all to the woman?” Jacob labored and toiled seven years and gave it all for Rachel, and counted it as nothing.

precepts.text: Many have run out of their wits for women and become servants for their sakes; Jacob served fourteen years for Rachel.
precepts.point: Men gather gold and silver and every goodly thing, then let all those things go and fix their eyes fast on a woman comely in favour and beauty. Many run out of their wits for a woman and become servants for their sakes; Jacob became a servant fourteen years, because he was deceived and served another seven.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
“Wherefore a man loveth his wife better than father or mother. Yea, many there be that have run out of their wits for women, and become servants for their sakes.”

Jacob is one of them. He became a servant for Rachel's sake, and not for seven years only: he was deceived and served another seven, so that he became a servant fourteen years for a woman. Seven years “seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her”; that is a man run out of his wits for a woman, exactly as the scripture says.

precepts.text: Favour is deceitful and beauty is vain, but a woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.
precepts.point: Favour is deceitful and beauty is vain. You are not going to look the same at seventy that you did at twenty-five; our days are threescore years and ten, or by reason of strength fourscore, and outside a handful who retain a semblance of their youth, the looks fade along the way. A woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
Jacob “loved also Rachel more than Leah”, and he was showing more favor to Rachel because he was more attracted to Rachel. “And when the Lord saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren.”

“Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.” Favor built on looks is deceitful, and beauty is vain because it does not last: you are not going to look the same at seventy that you did at twenty-five. The looks fade along the way, and the woman worth praising is the one that feareth the Lord. Leah, the hated one, is the one whose womb the Lord opened.

precepts.text: Our days are threescore years and ten, or by reason of strength fourscore years; the beauty of youth does not last the span.
precepts.point: Favour is deceitful and beauty is vain. You are not going to look the same at seventy that you did at twenty-five; our days are threescore years and ten, or by reason of strength fourscore, and outside a handful who retain a semblance of their youth, the looks fade along the way. A woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
“The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.”

Set that span against beauty. Seventy years, or eighty by reason of strength; and outside a handful who retain a semblance of their youth, the looks fade along the way. You are not going to look the same at seventy that you did at twenty-five. The beauty of youth does not last the span, which is why favour is deceitful and beauty is vain, and why Jacob loving Rachel more than Leah for her looks was building on something that passes.

precepts.text: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and Rachel was barren; Joseph and Benjamin were the only sons she brought forth.
precepts.point: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and Rachel was barren for years; she brought forth only Joseph and Benjamin. With Joseph presumed dead, Benjamin was the last son Jacob had of his beloved wife, so he would not let him go down.

note.label: Genesis 42: Joseph's Brethren Bow Down in Egypt

precepts.why:
“and he loved also Rachel more than Leah.” Jacob loved Rachel more, and served seven other years for her. “And when the Lord saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren.” Rachel was barren for years; she brought forth only two sons, Joseph and Benjamin.

With Joseph presumed dead, Benjamin was the last son Jacob had of his beloved wife. That is why he sent him not with his brethren, lest peradventure mischief befall him: he would not let the last son of Rachel go down.

precepts.text: Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days for the love he had for her.
precepts.point: Jacob fled into the country of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept sheep. That goes back to when Jacob served Laban for his wife.

note.label: Hosea 12: Ephraim Feedeth on the Wind

precepts.why: “Jacob fled into the country of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept sheep.” That goes back to when Jacob served Laban for his wife. “And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.” Serving for a wife and keeping sheep for a wife is those seven years for Rachel.

points: When Jacob saw Rachel he rolled the stone from the well's mouth and watered the flock, flexing like a bird puffing its chest, did she see me? Right away it altered his behavior. Abram and Isaac got married and went about God's business; Jacob lost his mind over Rachel. The kiss was a greeting, like the Northern Kingdom's kiss on the cheek, not making out.

note.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

points: Leah was tender eyed, but Rachel was beautiful and well favoured, and Jacob loved Rachel and served seven years that seemed but a few days for the love he had to her. Contrast Isaac: married, then loved. Jacob's love was based on physical beauty, emotional attraction, and romantic motivation, and what followed was deception, competition between Leah, Rachel, and the handmaids, and family tension. Scripture does not hide the cost of romance-driven decisions; it documents it.
